title: Working with individual bits
objective: By the end of this lesson you can set, clear, test, and toggle individual bits, and you can read the flag-manipulation code that appears throughout systems and security work.

blocks.text: Permissions, protocol headers, hardware registers, and compact option sets all pack several yes-or-no facts into one integer. The six operators in this lesson are how that packing and unpacking is done — and once you can read them, a whole layer of systems code stops looking cryptic.

rows: 1 only if both are 1 — used to test and to mask
1 if either is 1 — used to set
1 if they differ — used to toggle
moves bits up, filling with 0 — multiplies by 2^n
moves bits down — divides by 2^n for unsigned

blocks.caption: Seeing it in binary
lines: 1000      (8)      /* AND keeps only bits set in both */
1100  |  1010  =  1110   (14)   /* OR keeps bits set in either */

blocks.text: The four operations you will actually write

blocks.caption: Set, clear, toggle, test
lines: perms |= FLAG_READ | FLAG_WRITE;  /* set several at once */

blocks.title: Read &= ~MASK as 'keep everything except'
blocks.text: ~FLAG_WRITE is all ones except that one bit, so ANDing with it preserves every other flag and clears exactly one. This idiom appears constantly, and recognising it on sight — rather than working it out each time — is most of what makes flag code readable.

blocks.caption: Real examples
lines: /* File permissions, exactly as in the Linux course: */
/* Extracting fields from a packed header: */
unsigned int length  = header & 0xFFFF;        /* bottom 16 bits */

blocks.caption: Four ways this goes wrong
lines: /* 1 — & and | bind more loosely than == : parenthesise */
if (flags & MASK == 0)     { }    /* parsed as flags & (MASK == 0) — wrong */
/* 2 — shifting by the width or more is undefined */
unsigned int x = 1u << 32;        /* undefined on a 32-bit int */
/* 3 — right shift of a negative signed value is implementation-defined */
int  n = -8;  n >> 1;             /* result depends on the implementation */
if (a & b)  { }                   /* bitwise: 2 & 1 is 0, so this is false */
if (a && b) { }                   /* logical: both non-zero, so this is true */

blocks.title: Do bit work on unsigned types
blocks.text: Signed types bring in sign extension, implementation-defined right shifts, and undefined overflow — none of which you want when you are manipulating bit patterns. Declare flags, masks, and packed fields as unsigned int or uint32_t, and the whole category of surprises disappears.

blocks.caption: Idioms you will see
lines: x & (x - 1)            /* clears the lowest set bit — zero means power of two */
x | (x - 1)            /* sets all bits below the lowest set bit */
x & (alignment - 1)    /* offset within an alignment boundary, when alignment is a power of 2 */
while (x) { x &= x - 1; count++; }   /* one iteration per set bit */

blocks.title: Manipulate a flag set by hand
steps: Define FLAG_READ, FLAG_WRITE, FLAG_EXEC with (1u << n)
Write a function that prints a permission set as three characters, like rwx or r--
Set read and write, print; clear write, print; toggle exec twice, print
Write printf("%u\n", perms) after each step and watch the number change
Write a loop that prints all 32 bits of an unsigned int, most significant first
Try if (flags & MASK == 0) without parentheses and explain the result to yourself
Try 1u << 32 with -fsanitize=undefined and read the report
blocks.expected: A flag set you can read as both characters and a number, a bit printer you wrote yourself, and two of the classic traps triggered on purpose — including one the undefined-behaviour sanitizer names for you.

cheatsheet: << n multiplies by 2^n · >> n divides by 2^n for unsigned
Set: x |= MASK · Clear: x &= ~MASK · Toggle: x ^= MASK · Test: if (x & MASK)
Define flags as (1u << n) so each occupies one bit
Parenthesise: (flags & MASK) == 0, because & binds more loosely than ==
Shifting by the type's width or more is undefined
Do bit work on unsigned types — signed brings sign extension and undefined cases
& is bitwise and && is logical; they are not interchangeable
x & (x - 1) clears the lowest set bit — zero means x was a power of two

checkpoint.prompt: How do you clear a single flag while leaving the others untouched?
checkpoint.explanation: ~FLAG is all ones except that bit, so AND preserves everything else and clears exactly one. XOR would toggle it, which is different when it was already clear.

checkpoint.prompt: Why does if (flags & MASK == 0) not do what it looks like?

choices.B: == binds more tightly than &, so it is parsed as flags & (MASK == 0)
choices.C: & cannot be used in a condition

checkpoint.explanation: Precedence. Write (flags & MASK) == 0 — and note that -Wall usually warns about exactly this.

checkpoint.prompt: Why should bit manipulation use unsigned types?

choices.B: Signed types bring sign extension, implementation-defined right shift, and undefined overflow — none of which you want when working with bit patterns
choices.C: Signed types cannot be shifted at all
choices.D: It is required by the standard

checkpoint.explanation: Unsigned arithmetic is fully defined and wraps predictably, which is exactly the behaviour bit work assumes.

checkpoint.prompt: What does x & (x - 1) evaluating to zero tell you?

choices.B: x had at most one bit set — so it is zero or a power of two

checkpoint.explanation: Subtracting one flips the lowest set bit and everything below it; ANDing clears that bit. If nothing remains, there was only one bit to begin with.
